_: THE HTML LAW — how four blocks that share one address space make one web page: form (the elements), content (the words), style (the CSS), script (the JS). None names another; they agree on the address, and the reader reads across them at each one. The form says what kind of box stands at an address; the content at the same address is what the box holds. Read this law whole before reading any of the four.
1: ADDRESSES — the root of each block is the document. Its digits 1-9 are the document's parts in order; each part's digits are its own parts in order, and so down. A node is either a string (its line, with nothing beneath it) or an object whose '_' is its line and whose digits are its parts. The root's '_' in each of the four blocks is that block's title, never part of the page. The same address names the same place in all four blocks. In the content, style and script blocks a node that only carries the way down to deeper digits may have no '_' at all.
2: THE FORM'S LINES — a line is an element's tag name: 'p', 'div', 'a', 'svg'. When the element has attributes, its '_' is itself an object — the node's hidden directory: that inner '_' is the tag, and the inner digits are the attributes in their order, each written name="value" with the value raw (nothing escaped) — the value runs from the first quote to the last, so a quote inside it needs nothing — or the bare name alone when the value is empty. An attribute written as its name and '=' with nothing after (alt=, title=, aria-label=, placeholder=, a description meta's content=, style=, onclick=) keeps its value in another block, at the same hidden address: words a person reads in the content, inline CSS in the style, inline handlers in the script (3, 5). The hidden directory holds no parts; the node's parts are the digits beside the '_', never inside it. A line beginning '!--' is a comment and the rest of the line is its text. A line beginning '!DOCTYPE' is the doctype. A line that is exactly '…' is no element at all: see 6.
3: THE CONTENT — at an address where the form has an element: if the content there is a string, it is the element's only child, its text. If the content there is an object, then each of its digits that the form does NOT have at that address is a run of text standing at that place among the element's parts, and each digit the form DOES have is the content of that part, read by this same rule. An element the content does not mention holds no text. Where the element's form line has routed attributes (2), the content node's '_' is an object — its hidden directory — holding each attribute's words at the same hidden digit as in the form; if the element is a string leaf, its text then stands at that hidden directory's own '_'. Otherwise a '_' in the content that is a string, anywhere but the root, is a summary slot: it is for readers of the block and is never printed on the page.
4: ASSEMBLY — walk the form from the root, parts in digit order 1 to 9. At an element emit '<' tag, then each attribute (a space, then name="value" with & written & and " written ", or the bare name), then '>'; then its parts in digit order — wherever the form has no part at a digit but the content has a string there, emit that text; then '</' tag '>'. Void elements — area base br col embed hr img input link meta source track wbr — get no end tag and have no parts. Escape text: & as &, < as <, > as >; inside title and textarea escape only & and <. Emit a comment as <!--text--> and the doctype as <!DOCTYPE html>. Write no whitespace of your own between elements. A browser drops one newline straight after <pre>, <textarea> or <listing>, so when such an element's text begins with a newline, write one more.
5: CODE — at the address of a <style> element the style block holds its CSS; at the address of a <script> element the script block holds its JS. Emit each exactly as written between its tags, never escaped. The CSS and the JS never stand in the content block; the content block is only the words a person reads. An element's inline style attribute keeps its CSS in the style block's hidden directory at the element's address, and an inline handler keeps its JS in the script block's the same way.
6: SUPERNESTS — no node has more than nine parts. An element with more than nine lays them nine to a group: its digit 1 is a '…' node holding parts 1-9, its digit 2 a '…' node holding parts 10-18, and so on; past eighty-one, groups of groups. When assembling, emit a '…' node's parts in its place with no tag of its own — the page never sees the group. The content follows the same groups at the same addresses, and a group's '_' in the content is its summary slot. Attributes past nine fold the same way inside the hidden directory.
7: TAKING A PAGE APART (the other direction) — parse as a browser does: the document always holds html, and html always holds head then body, whether or not the source wrote them. Whitespace: collapse every run of spaces, tabs and newlines in text to one space, except inside pre, textarea, script and style, which keep theirs exactly; drop a text run that is only whitespace when it sits between two block-level elements (or between one and the start or end of its parent) — html, head, body, div, p, section, article, header, footer, nav, main, aside, ul, ol, li, dl, dt, dd, table and its parts, h1-h6, form, fieldset, figure, figcaption, blockquote, hr, pre, details, summary, script, style, link, meta, title; trim the space at a text run's edge that touches such an element or the edge of such a parent. A single space between two inline elements stays: it is a word space. Every remaining text run is content; every element, comment and the doctype is form; a style's text goes to the style block and a script's to the script block, each at its element's own address. An element whose only child is one text run gets that text as a string in the content at its own address.
9: PROVENANCE — written 25 October 2026 by weft (Claude Code, a keyless cloud session, lane code-as-blocks) as the law for an experiment: whether code can be taken apart into pscale blocks. Run against the site's own pages first: 134 of 134 at happyseaurchin.com taken apart into these four blocks and put back exactly, eight of eight checked pixel for pixel in Chromium. Refined the same day from the first agent to assemble a page by this law alone, which named where it had to guess (2, 4). And from the first agent to take a page apart by it, whose blocks matched the code's at every position (1). Extended the same day so that every byte goes to the block of its kind: words hiding in attributes (about 1,150 across the site) to the content, inline styles to the style (2, 3, 5).
